disclaimer: Typical adult reference ranges; labs vary; not for clinical decisions.

sources.guyton: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th edition. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2021.
sources.accaha2017: Whelton PK, Carey RM, Aronow WS, et al. 2017 ACC/AHA/AAPA/ABC/ACPM/AGS/APhA/ASH/ASPC/NMA/PCNA Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults: A Report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Clinical Practice Guidelines. Hypertension. 2018;71(6):e13-e115.

values.label: Mean arterial pressure
values.where: Chapter 14, Overview of the Circulation; Biophysics of Pressure, Flow, and Resistance: 'Pressures in the Various Portions of the Circulation' (mean pressure in the aorta averages about 100 mm Hg)
values.note: Single typical value; the source gives no range.

values.label: Systolic arterial pressure (young adult)
values.where: Chapter 15, Vascular Distensibility and Functions of the Arterial and Venous Systems: 'Arterial Pressure Pulsations' (in the healthy young adult, systolic pressure about 120 mm Hg)

values.label: Diastolic arterial pressure (young adult)
values.where: Chapter 15, Vascular Distensibility and Functions of the Arterial and Venous Systems: 'Arterial Pressure Pulsations' (in the healthy young adult, diastolic pressure about 80 mm Hg)

values.label: Heart rate
values.where: Chapter 9, Cardiac Muscle; The Heart as a Pump and Function of the Heart Valves: 'Cardiac Cycle' (duration of the cycle at a normal heart rate of 72 beats/min)

values.label: Stroke volume
values.where: Chapter 9, 'End-Diastolic Volume, End-Systolic Volume, and Stroke Volume Output' (about 70 mL)
values.note: Single typical value; the source gives no range.

values.label: Cardiac output (resting)
values.where: Chapter 20, Cardiac Output, Venous Return, and Their Regulation: 'Normal Values for Cardiac Output at Rest and During Activity' (about 5 L/min in the resting adult)
values.note: Single typical value; it varies with body size, activity and age.

values.label: Total peripheral resistance
values.where: Chapter 14, Overview of the Circulation; Biophysics of Pressure, Flow, and Resistance: 'Total Peripheral Vascular Resistance and Total Pulmonary Vascular Resistance' (flow about 100 mL/s and a systemic pressure difference of about 100 mm Hg give a total peripheral resistance of about 100/100, or 1 peripheral resistance unit)
values.note: PRU: peripheral resistance unit, mm Hg of pressure difference per mL/s of flow. The source rounds resting flow up to 100 mL/s for this example.

states.label: Calcium channel blockers
states.summary: They reduce calcium entry into the muscle of the arteriole walls, which needs calcium to contract, and blood pressure falls.
states.where: Section 8.1.6, Choice of Initial Medication, Table 18 (Oral Antihypertensive Drugs), primary agents: dihydropyridine and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are listed as blood-pressure-lowering agents.
states.modelNote: Only the pressure direction is cited. The model shows the artery-relaxing kind as lower arteriole tone, so its resistance falls and the baroreflex speeds the heart a little. That illustrates the background physiology in Guyton and Hall, Chapter 17, 'Vascular Control by Ions and Other Chemical Factors' (an increase in calcium ion concentration causes vasoconstriction by stimulating smooth muscle contraction); it is not a cited direction for the drug class, and heart-slowing members of the class differ.

states.label: Alpha-1 blockers
states.summary: Sympathetic signals can no longer tighten arterioles through alpha-1 receptors, so resistance and pressure fall.
states.where: Chapter 18, Nervous Regulation of the Circulation and Rapid Control of Arterial Pressure, 'Norepinephrine: The Sympathetic Vasoconstrictor Transmitter Substance': the substance secreted at the vasoconstrictor nerve endings is almost entirely norepinephrine, which acts directly on the alpha-adrenergic receptors of the vascular smooth muscle to cause vasoconstriction. Blocking those receptors removes that vasoconstriction, which lowers resistance and, at a given flow, pressure (Chapter 14, 'Interrelationships of Pressure, Flow, and Resistance'). Pressure: ACC/AHA 2017 guideline, Section 8.1.6, Table 18 (Oral Antihypertensive Drugs), secondary agents, which lists alpha-1 blockers among blood-pressure-lowering agents.
states.modelNote: In the model the baroreflex also speeds the heart a little; that is model behaviour, not a listed direction.

states.label: Central alpha-2 agonists
states.summary: They act in the brainstem to turn down sympathetic outflow, and pressure falls.
states.where: Section 8.1.6, Choice of Initial Medication, Table 18 (Oral Antihypertensive Drugs), secondary agents: 'Central alpha2-agonist and other centrally acting drugs' are listed as blood-pressure-lowering agents.
states.modelNote: Only the pressure direction is cited. The model's slower heart, lower output and lower resistance illustrate turning down sympathetic outflow, using Guyton and Hall, Chapter 18, 'Vasomotor Center in the Brain and Its Control of the Vasoconstrictor System' (sympathetic signals from the vasomotor center raise heart rate and contractility and constrict vessels); they are not cited directions. Because the drug acts in the brainstem, where the baroreflex is wired, the model also lowers the pressure the reflex defends, so the reflex does not speed the heart back up.

states.label: Beta-blockers
states.summary: Sympathetic signals reach the heart less, so it beats more slowly and squeezes less, lowering cardiac output and pressure.
states.where: Heart rate and output: Chapter 9, Cardiac Muscle; The Heart as a Pump and Function of the Heart Valves, 'Control of the Heart by the Sympathetic and Parasympathetic Nerves' (decreasing sympathetic stimulation decreases heart rate and strength of contraction, lowering cardiac pumping), the effect that blocking the heart's beta receptors produces. Pressure: ACC/AHA 2017 guideline, Section 8.1.6, Table 18 (Oral Antihypertensive Drugs), which lists beta blockers among blood-pressure-lowering agents.
states.modelNote: In the model the baroreflex tightens arterioles a little as output falls, so resistance rises; no resistance direction is listed.

states.label: Direct vasodilators
states.summary: They relax arteriole muscle directly; resistance and pressure fall, the baroreflex speeds the heart, and over days the kidneys retain salt and water.
states.where: Section 8.1.6, Choice of Initial Medication, Table 18 (Oral Antihypertensive Drugs), secondary agents, direct vasodilators: listed as blood-pressure-lowering agents; comment: 'Associated with sodium and water retention and reflex tachycardia; use with a diuretic and beta blocker.' Resistance falls with arteriolar dilation (Guyton and Hall, Chapter 14, 'Interrelationships of Pressure, Flow, and Resistance').
states.modelNote: The model shows only the immediate response. It does not simulate the later sodium and water retention that the guideline comment describes.

states.label: Hemorrhage (volume loss)
states.summary: Lost blood means less blood returns to the heart, so cardiac output and arterial pressure fall; sympathetic reflexes speed the heart.
states.where: Chapter 24, Circulatory Shock and Its Treatment: 'Shock Caused by Hypovolemia: Hemorrhagic Shock', 'Relationship of Bleeding Volume to Cardiac Output and Arterial Pressure' and 'Sympathetic Reflex Compensations in Shock' (increased heart rate)
states.modelNote: In the model, blood per beat also falls with less filling and the baroreflex tightens arterioles, so resistance rises; those are model behaviour, not listed directions.
